lesson.title: The Spectrum Analyzer: Seeing Frequency Instead of Time
lesson.summary: A spectrum analyzer displays a signal's amplitude versus frequency rather than voltage versus time, revealing the individual frequency components, the frequency spectrum, that make up a waveform.
lesson.body:
An oscilloscope answers the question "what does this voltage look like moment to moment?" A spectrum analyzer answers a different question: "which frequencies is this signal actually made of, and how strong is each one?" Instead of plotting voltage against time, its horizontal axis is frequency and its vertical axis is amplitude, often in decibels. Every repeating, non sinusoidal waveform can be broken down into a sum of sine waves at different frequencies, a fundamental frequency plus a series of harmonics at whole number multiples of it, and that decomposition is exactly what the frequency spectrum describes. A spectrum analyzer displays each of those component frequencies as a distinct peak, or spike, at its corresponding position on the horizontal axis, with the peak's height showing how much of that frequency is present.

A square wave makes the contrast especially clear. On an oscilloscope, a 1 kHz square wave looks exactly like what its name suggests: a flat topped signal alternating cleanly between two voltage levels. Feed that same signal into a spectrum analyzer, and the screen shows something quite different: a tall peak at 1 kHz, the fundamental, a smaller peak at 3 kHz, a smaller one still at 5 kHz, and so on, at every odd multiple of the fundamental, with each successive harmonic weaker than the last. None of that internal structure is visible in the time domain trace on a scope; the square wave's sharp corners are, mathematically, the product of adding together all of those sine waves at once. The spectrum analyzer is what lets you see the ingredients rather than just the finished shape.

In practice, this makes a spectrum analyzer especially useful for finding things a time domain trace hides: unwanted harmonics generated by a nonlinear circuit, interference from a nearby signal at a specific frequency, or noise that only shows up as a small bump on a much larger fundamental peak. Where the oscilloscope tells you what a signal does, the spectrum analyzer tells you what a signal is made of.
